question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was involved in a motorcycle collision. He was not wearing a helmet. Physical examination shows left periorbital ecchymosis. A CT scan of the head shows a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. Physical examination of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

options.ope: Complete loss of vision of the left eye

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone" -> "Compression of the left superior orbital fissure" -> "Involvement of cranial nerves III, IV, V1, VI" -> "Numbness of the left cheek" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone" -> "Compression of the left superior orbital fissure" -> "Involvement of cranial nerves III, IV, V1, VI" -> "Possible impairment of eye movement" -> "Preserved left lateral gaze" -> 60%

CHAIN: "Fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone" -> "Compression of the left superior orbital fissure" -> "Involvement of cranial nerves III, IV, V1, VI" -> "Possible impairment of corneal reflex" -> "Absent left corneal reflex" -> 70%

CHAIN: "Fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone" -> "Compression of the left superior orbital fissure" -> "Involvement of cranial nerves III, IV, V1, VI" -> "Possible optic nerve involvement" -> "Complete loss of vision of the left eye" -> 50%

CHAIN: "Fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone" -> "Compression of the left superior orbital fissure" -> "Involvement of cranial nerves III, IV, V1, VI" -> "No direct involvement of olfactory nerve" -> "Decreased sense of smell unlikely" -> 40%
analysis: The fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure suggests a superior orbital fissure syndrome. This condition typically affects cranial nerves III, IV, V1 (ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve), and VI. The symptoms can include ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, proptosis, and sensory loss in the distribution of the ophthalmic nerve. The preserved left lateral gaze would indicate that the abducens nerve (CN VI) is functioning, which is unlikely in this scenario. Numbness of the left cheek would involve the maxillary branch (V2) of the trigeminal nerve, which is not affected in superior orbital fissure syndrome. The absent left corneal reflex would be due to involvement of the ophthalmic branch (V1) of the trigeminal nerve, which is consistent with superior orbital fissure syndrome.
